newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Navy floats unisex warship.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Navy floats unisex warship.

text.p: Six years after the Tailhook scandal, the Navy is commissioning its first ship designed to accommodate both male and female crew members.

USS The Sullivans, named after five brothers who perished when their Navy cruiser was sunk during World War Two, is an Aegis destroyer that its executive officer, Lt. Cmdr. Steve Davis, describes as "the Maserati of ships."
The four gas turbine engines aboard, the same as those used on a DC-10 aircraft, can propel the 505-foot-long, 8,500 ton vessel from zero to 30 knots in 90 seconds.
The engineer responsible for making sure those engines and a number of other complex systems work is a nine-year Navy veteran, Lt. Esther McClure.

"I have never been treated with anything less than professionalism," said McClure, the senior woman officer on the ship and third in the chain of command. "It's all a question of what you bring to the table.

"If you're a competent professional, then that's how you're treated," said the 34-year-old McClure, who has previously served in the Pacific and also in Desert Storm. "I look at this as a great opportunity. It's a chance to step up to the plate and feel like I'm very much a member of the team."

She supervises a crew of 60, six of whom are women. "Engineering is not typically something women do," said McClure, who has lived in many places around the globe, and considers Austin, Texas, home. But engineering is one career path officers can follow to get command of their own ship.
The Sullivans' commanding officer, Cmdr. Gerard Roncolato, served as an engineer early in his naval career.
"We've had women from the very beginning on this ship," he said, noting McClure was the third person selected to be part of the 314-member crew three years ago.

The crew, which was training ashore near the Bath Iron Works factory in Maine where the steel-hulled vessel was built for about $900 million, has been living aboard The Sullivans since January. It sailed to the Naval War College in Rhode Island for further exercises last month and will be formally commissioned April 19 in New York City.

"When Admiral (Jeremy) Boorda ordered the practice of sending women to sea accelerated, other ships were retrofitted, but this one was built with the assumption that women would be part of the crew," Roncolato said.

A ship's crew is "a very tight unit and on other vessels they've injected a group of women into the crew," Roncolato said. "Here, they've become an intergral part and it's worked out very well. We've really had very little problems."

Just as the Aegis radar aboard continually searches the skies and can detect a quarter tossed from small plane flying 250 miles away, the commander said he was vigilant about any charges of sexual harassment or fraternisation.
"We use the motto that the actions of one of us affect the lives of all of us and that goes not just for gender issues, but all issues aboard ship," he said.
Indeed, the actions by drunken naval pilots and sailors that turned the 1991 Tailhook convention into a vicious bacchanal in which 83 women were assaulted had severe consequences.
The Navy is still trying to recover from Tailhook, which resulted in disciplinary action against a number of sailors and forced the Chief of Naval Operations at the time into early retirement.
Since then, as more women have gone to sea, there have been reports of sailors becoming pregnant while serving aboard ships.
Roncolato said, "This ship is too small. At one time or another everyone is under everyone else's chain of command, so dating shipmates is not permitted."
While he, Davis and McClure have all served aboard ships before, a number of the enlisted personnel have not and the cramped quarters, whether for men or women, is something they are getting used to.

"It's been an adjustment," Yeoman Gail Choyce, 37, from Saginaw, Michigan, said of her quarters which she shares with 17 other women. "There's one toilet, one shower and when reveille sounds, you just have to stand in line."
